title: A professional project proposal
body: One document, structured the way a client actually reads: what they told you they need, what you propose doing about it, what it costs, and what happens next. No twelve-page preamble about your studio's founding story.
pointOne: Cover page carrying their brand, not yours
pointTwo: Summary a non-technical buyer can follow
pointThree: Approach section drawn from the scope
sample: Northbeam needs the new site live before the spring campaign. This proposal covers a six-page build, the blog migration, and a two-week buffer ahead of launch.

title: Scope of work and deliverables
body: The section that quietly decides whether the project is profitable. Pilot turns the brief into deliverables with edges — what is included, what is explicitly not, and what trips a change order.
pointThree: Change-order trigger on every soft line
pointFour: Assumptions written down before they bite
sample: Included: six unique page templates. Not included: ongoing content entry, third-party licences, or copywriting beyond the migrated posts.

title: Suggested pricing packages
body: Three options, because one number invites a negotiation and two invite a coin flip. Pilot anchors the set so the middle package reads as the sensible choice, and shows you the arithmetic behind each one.
pointThree: Per-line pricing you can defend out loud
sample: Complete — $9,800. Six pages, blog migration, two revision rounds, and four weeks of post-launch support.

title: Project milestones and timeline
body: Dates the client agrees to before the work starts, with their own obligations written in. Most overruns are feedback delays wearing a costume, and a schedule that names the reviewer stops the argument early.
pointThree: Dependencies flagged before they surprise you
pointFour: Slip rules tied back to your terms
sample: Design review closes Friday 14 March. Feedback arriving after this date moves launch by one week.

title: Contract-ready terms
body: The paragraphs you keep meaning to write properly. Deposit, revisions, cancellation, IP transfer, late payment — in plain language, checked against the norms of the place you are billing from.
sample: Ownership of all delivered work transfers on receipt of the final payment. Until then the licence is limited to review.

title: Follow-up emails
body: The part everyone skips, and the part that closes. Three drafts, already scheduled, that read like a person following up rather than a sequence firing on a timer.
pointOne: Day three, day eight, day fifteen
pointTwo: Tone matched to the original thread
pointFour: Open tracking on the proposal link
sample: Hi Dana — no rush at all. Did the middle package look about right, or would it help if I put together something leaner?

title: Client questionnaires
body: Sent before you quote, not after you have already underpriced. Eight questions calibrated to the project type, surfacing the budget, the decision-maker, and the deadline nobody thought to mention.
pointOne: A question set per project type
pointFour: Answers flow straight into the scope
sample: Who signs this off — and is there anyone else whose opinion will matter in week five?
